name: Seed-Mirage
description: Seed-Mirage is a desert world of extremes, where glass plains left by an ancient cataclysm stretch for thousands of kilometers, their mirror surfaces creating optical illusions that make navigation by sight unreliable. The glass reflects the sky so perfectly that the horizon vanishes, and distant features appear to float in midair. Dust seas border the glass plains, their dunes advancing and retreating across the vitrified surface in cycles driven by seasonal winds. Near the geothermal vents, rare plants cling to existence in soil pockets where moisture condenses from the heated air.

The heat on Seed-Mirage is magnified by the glass plains, which absorb and re-radiate solar energy with devastating efficiency. The center of a glass plain at midday can reach temperatures that exceed what the atmospheric models predict, as the reflective surface creates a greenhouse effect in the air layer immediately above it. The edges of the glass, where dust has encroached, produce the most spectacular mirages, layered inversions that project distant landscapes into the sky. The flora that survives does so in the margins, the narrow strips where conditions are merely harsh rather than lethal.

The cataclysm that created the glass plains left radiation hotspots that persist after geological ages, suggesting an event of extraordinary energy. The glass contains embedded seeds from the biosphere that existed before the event, preserved in a vitrified state that has maintained their cellular structures intact. Xenobotanists have successfully germinated some of these ancient seeds, discovering plant species of remarkable complexity and beauty that have been extinct for millions of years. The current flora appears to be a degraded remnant of this earlier biosphere, hanging on in conditions far harsher than those its ancestors evolved for.

The ancient seeds in the glass represent a biological archive of incalculable value, containing the genetic information of an entire lost biosphere. Proposals to use these seeds to re-vegetate Seed-Mirage have clashed with concerns that the radiation hotspots may make large-scale restoration impossible, and that the modern conditions are simply too harsh for the ancient species. Meanwhile, the existing flora continues its decline, and each year the advancing dunes bury more of the glass and the seeds it contains. The planet is simultaneously a graveyard and a seed bank, holding life in suspension while the conditions for that life slowly disappear.
